- Under the law of torts, a person may sue a third party without having a contract with that party.
- In the case of someone who is injured by a product, tort law can impose liability on everyone who contributed to the manufacture and sale of the product.
- A company whose product injures a bystander may be held liable without a contract.
- The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enforces laws against unfair or deceptive practices and provides free resources for consumers and companies.
- The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) offers guidance on advertising and marketing rules, data security, and privacy.
- IdentityTheft.gov can help victims report identity theft and build recovery plans.
- In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act generally shields online platforms from liability for content posted by their users.
- Strict liability can attach to the manufacture, storage, or sale of defective products.
- Product liability laws often rely on the concept of strict liability.
- Products liability laws can attach to all stages of a product's manufacture, storage, and sale.
- A store that fails to clean a spill after being warned may be found negligent.
- A delivery driver who causes a crash, a website that publishes a false accusation, or a manufacturer whose product injures a bystander can face liability without any contract.

The task force, which was created by the Legislature in 2013, is made up of physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts who review individual maternal deaths case by case.
Results of the task force’s early analysis were startling. Although Black women account for about one in nine births in Texas, they experienced nearly three in ten maternal deaths. The numbers were striking enough to prompt a more rigorous review, which showed that data and reporting errors had inflated some of those figures. But in a later analysis, researchers reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology that Texas’ maternal mortality rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011. That increase was far steeper than in comparable states.
What’s driving that increase?
The task force has also found that Texas does not collect critical data about maternal outcomes. The task force also aims to address systemic issues.
The task force’s extension is on the special session’s agenda, but the panel’s members want to go further. Texas Medicaid covers about half of the state’s births, and Texas has some of the strictest income limits in the country for parents eligible for pregnancy-related Medicaid.
The task force recommends that the Legislature allow women to continue to receive Medicaid benefits up to a year after delivery.
Texas also did not expand Medicaid as part of the federal health care law.
The task force’s recommendations, designed to help prevent maternal deaths, also include more comprehensive coverage for mental health care, particularly for low-income mothers.

It has been on my mind off and on for years.
It still remains my list of essentials.
Here is my list, along with a few explanations, and a couple of examples.
Hello. The first time someone introduced me as “my friend,” this phrase felt so large. I believe in you.
Help/Danger. The word “danger” can be a warning, or an alert to not only protect others, but to keep a person safe. Cooking, driving across town, remembering birthdays can leave doubt.
Trust/Believe. I’ve paired these two, because, for me, they are inseparable.
Friend. To be a friend, means to be there for someone.
Always.
“Hello. Always.”
Khalil Gibran once imagined, in a thought experiment attributed to his writings, language reduced to only seven words. Seven words to express the human experience, emotions, desires, and interactions.
What seven words would you choose?

A common claim says that 7% of all meaning lives outside the words we speak; 38% in the tone we speak them in; and 55% in body language.
These figures come from Albert Mehrabian's studies in the late 1960's, which aimed to measure how people judged feelings and attitudes when someone's words clashed with their tone or expression. Mehrabian never claimed that 93% of all meaning lived outside language. So why is the 7% rule so prevalent?
In many situations, watching someone speak can provide real insights into their meaning.
We even naturally synchronise our movements and gestures to create a rapport.
There are situations where body language matters just as much, if not more, than the words we speak. Someone who apologises to you while looking away and fiddling with their phone lands an insult, not an apology.
Next time you're delivering a talk or presentation, consider how your body language is affecting your audience. You can use your hands to emphasise certain points.
Yet even in situations where body language is vital, the words we speak are just as important.
The 7% rule overlooks the importance of words in favour of body language. But words and body language are deeply intertwined. They form an integrated system that allows us to share meaning and thoughts with each other. It's only when we focus on body language as a concept, separate from the words we speak, that we make mistakes.
The important message here is that there is no 7% rule.

For example, the gross domestic product (GDP) of Country A is four times that of Country B, indicating that Country A has greater output. If Country A has a population of 200 million, while Country B has a population of 10 million, then the average resident of Country B has access to far more goods and services than the average resident of Country A.
The underground economy consists of legal goods and services exchanged off the books in order to avoid taxes or regulation, such as cash-paid babysitting or unreported tips.
GDP does not measure many important aspects of life. Clearing a forest for timber raises GDP now, while the lost ecosystem services and long-term sustainability are not recorded as a cost. Cleanup after an environmental disaster can increase GDP, because the spending on repair and remediation counts as production.
GDP does not measure human capital, which is the skills and health of the labor force.
Economists who use GDP as a measure of well-being are counting only the flow of production and consumption, and they are ignoring other dimensions of economic well-being, such as the amount of leisure time for which people have a choice or the health of the people. For example, in a country where the top 1 percent of households earns half of all income, GDP per capita might look healthy but the typical household might be struggling.

These hormones are made out of the thyroid gland, using iodine from the diet.
Seaweed is promoted as a superfood by many natural health advocates, and it shows up all over the place in the natural health world.
You might take a kelp capsule, a "thyroid support" blend, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt without adding up the total iodine. Too much iodine can cause problems, particularly in people who have thyroid problems.
Seaweed is just one source of iodine.
Many estimates put Japan's average daily iodine intake at one to several milligrams per day, well above Western upper limits.
But more careful studies show that iodine from seaweed in Japan is not the steady, high, supplement-like dose that you get when you take a kelp capsule.
In Japan seaweed is eaten as part of meals, in varied types and amounts. Japanese iodine intake swings from day to day, which allows the body to accommodate high iodine intake.
One small pinch of kombu can exceed a day's upper limit for iodine, and some samples contain several times that. Nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu.
That's been documented in Japan, particularly among heavy consumers of kombu.
Many Japanese clinicians often advise patients with certain thyroid conditions to limit seaweed.
What does this mean for us?
Hijiki can contain high levels of inorganic arsenic, and several food-safety agencies advise against eating it.
The common alga spirulina is often promoted as a vitamin B12 source, but much of its B12 is a form that humans can't use.
A single gram of dried kombu can contain more than a thousand micrograms of iodine, and some samples contain several times that.
What about other algae?
Microalgae are single-celled organisms.
And there are also microcystins (liver toxins from other cyanobacteria) to worry about if the microalgae aren't grown under the best conditions.
Microalgae products have been promoted as a source of omega-3 fatty acids, and several algal oils already supply DHA in supplements and infant formula.
The Japanese tradition is that high iodine can be tolerated in context. This tradition does not show that a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult raised on a low-iodine diet.
In conclusion, we advise caution.

- The defining credit bubble example is the 2008 financial crisis, when bank stocks collapsed and credit froze. The S&P 500 fell more than 50% from its 2007 peak to its March 2009 low.
- The classic economic bubble case is Japan in the late 1980’s, when soaring stock and real estate prices made the country feel invincible. The Nikkei index peaked at the end of 1989 and did not return to that level for more than 30 years, while the economy stagnated for years afterward.
- A classic market bubble example is the housing boom of the mid-2000’s, when home prices rose year after year and many buyers assumed they always would. When home values started falling in 2007-2008, banks, builders, and insurers got hit first. The wider stock market dragged down sharply.
- The textbook stock market bubble is the dot-com bubble of the late 1990’s, when investors poured money into internet companies, many with no profits and sometimes barely a business plan. The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and lost roughly three-quarters of its value over the next couple of years.
- The bubble burst when oil spiked to nearly $150 a barrel in 2008, then collapsed below $40.
- The Nasdaq took until 2015 to regain its 2000 peak.

Gaucher disease is an inherited disorder that results in the accumulation of a fatty substance called glucocerebroside.
This substance builds up in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, and sometimes in other organs, including the brain.
The team compared mice that modeled neuronopathic Gaucher disease with control mice and exposed both groups to the virus. They found that the neuronopathic mice had greater resistance to Sindbis infection in the brain.
Sindbis virus is a mosquito-borne alphavirus that scientists widely use in laboratory research as a model of viral infection of the central nervous system.
Certain variants of the GBA gene, which we inherit from our parents, increase the risk of developing Gaucher disease.
These variants affect the way that the body breaks down fatty substances, such as glucocerebroside. As a result, these substances accumulate in the body.
For this reason, scientists are keen to learn more about the factors that affect this gene and how variants of it affect the body.
The researchers were particularly interested in understanding how the brain’s immune response to Gaucher disease affects its resistance to viral infection.
The team modeled the full neuronopathic disease in their mouse models, which developed the most severe symptoms of neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
The researchers then investigated which mechanisms might explain the increased resistance to the virus in the brains of the Gaucher mice. They determined that the pre-existing type I interferon response — which occurs before infection — offered the protection.
According to the authors, “These findings suggest that the brain’s immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make the mouse brains more resistant to infection with Sindbis virus.”
The researchers write that their findings demonstrate the “protective role of preexisting type I interferon in the brain’s immune response.”
The researchers highlight that the sickle cell trait offering some protection against malaria is the best-known example of such an advantage.
Also, the authors note that carrier rates of GBA variants are notably elevated in certain populations, including Ashkenazi Jews.
The team plan to continue their research into the protective aspects of Gaucher disease.

- In this article, we shall try to get a glimpse into the evolution of marriage throughout history. Going back to ancient Roman civilization, we shall understand how marriage was viewed then and take an overview of how marriage has evolved over the years.
- In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, marriage was formally established as one of the seven sacraments.
- The Council of Traditional Council in 1215 which further tightened the rules on marriage including the public announcement of the intended marriages and hence curbing the secret unions and also clarifying the issue of who was legitimately wed.
- Roman marriage required consent and the intention to live as husband and wife, called affectio maritalis
The evolution of marriage can be well understood from the following lines:
- This was an important social institution, which was regulated and controlled by the state as well as the church.
- Marriage was the legal union between a man and a woman with the object of forming a family.
- Marriage was part of the Roman law before the Christianity existed.
- The earliest Roman marriages did not require a formal ceremony.
- The concept of marriage has evolved throughout history.
Marriage has however, undergone a sea change over the centuries. It has evolved in meaning and definition as well. Let us see how the concept of marriage has undergone change over the years:
- Marriages in ancient Rome were different from those which take place today. Marriages in ancient Rome were conducted for various reasons like increase in property, increasing family, social and political status etc.

Stimming is an activity or behavior that is the self-regulatory, repetitive, rhythmic, and stereotyped mannerisms often associated with autism.
All of us fidget in one way or another to help us cope with the stresses of daily life. People with autism spectrum disorder (S.D.) may also engage in these repetitive and self-regulating behaviors, although the nature of these behaviors may differ from those engaged in by their neurotypical peers.
They may also be engaged in to increase arousal, especially when bored or at a time when sensory input is needed.
The term “stim” is derived from the word “self-stimulatory behavior”. These behaviors may vary in intensity, frequency, or even repetitiveness. They may involve movements, such as flapping the hands, rocking, twirling, spinning, or pacing.
A person may also engage in repetitive behaviors to help them think, such as pacing while thinking or biting their nails while deep in thought.
While you may refer to all these behaviors as “stimming”, it’s important to know that there are several types of stimming.
Here are a few examples of stims, as well as some reasons why someone may engage in them:
Hands: Flicker fingers, hand flapping, nail biting
Many people with autism may rock their hands back and forth, flicker their fingers, or even bite their nails.
These self-stimulatory behaviors may serve to relieve stress, release tension, or even increase arousal levels. They may also be engaged in to help a person on the autism spectrum pay attention and concentrate.
Hands: Finger playing
Some individuals on the autism spectrum may engage in finger play to help them concentrate. They may also engage in finger play to help them think.
Hands: Chewing
Many children with autism may engage in self-stimulatory behavior, such as chewing on their hands. They may also engage in these behaviors to relieve tension, release stress, or increase arousal levels.
Hands: Scratching
People with autism may engage in self-stimulatory behaviors, such as scratching themselves. They may also engage in these behaviors to relieve tension or stress.
Hands: Tapping
Some individuals on the autism spectrum may engage in self-stimulatory behaviors, such as tapping their hands on a table, door, or even the wall.
Buttresses: Pacing
Some individuals with autism may engage in self-stimulatory behaviors, such as pacing.
The stimming behaviors often are not dangerous to the person or others. However, there are some stimming behaviors that can cause a person to injure themselves.
Some of these include:
Exploring a surface with the hands and fingers
Pushing or rubbing on the face or body
Tap or flick a finger or hand
Pace or walk in a repetitive manner
Repeatedly tapping an object on a surface
Finger-snapping or hand-flapping
Biting the skin around the fingers or the finger itself
Biting the lips or chewing the tongue
Flapping, twisting, flicking, or rubbing of the fingers
It is usually done to help regulate their emotions.
Stimming may be done in order to calm down, relieve stress, or provide sensory input. Stimming can also occur as a result of boredom or to help pass the time.
Stimming may be a way to help regulate emotions, it is typically not harmful to the individual engaging in this behavior.
This behavior can be self-injurious, or it can cause them to hurt themselves.

A lot of attention is spent on the technical and accountancy-specific know-how required by accounting students. Yet, the importance of communication skills is often overlooked. However, clear communication skills are crucial for accountants at all stages of their career.
CPA, ACCA, and CIMA exams all include written components where the quality of communication affects the score. In short, this is something to take very seriously.
This article provides a checklist that you can use as a guide to improve the quality of your communication skills.
A good thesis is focussed, arguable and supported by evidence.
For example, the thesis:
The impact of fair value measurement on bank earnings volatility during the 2008 crisis
is focussed, arguable, and supported by evidence.
The thesis:
Revenue may be recognized when the goods are delivered
It would be more effective to say “Revenue must be recognized when the goods are delivered”. In other words, you’re expected to make value judgements and argue your case.
State assumptions explicitly
When answering questions on standards such as IFRS 15 or ASC 842, it’s important to reference relevant principles by name.
However, it’s also essential to state the assumptions underpinning your conclusions.
For example, to conclude that inventory is not impaired, you may write “Assuming the inventory is not impaired…”. Similarly, to conclude that inventory is impaired, you may write “Assuming the inventory is impaired…”
Use the correct terms
Consider the following statements:
The transaction will be recognized in the accounts as a material misstatement.
The transaction will be recognized in the accounts as a misstatement.
A “material misstatement” and “misstatement” describe two different situations.
It’s also important to use the correct terms, for example “accrued” and “deferred” describe different situations.
Use the correct words
For example, “may” and “must” describe different situations. You “may” do something or you “may not” do something. You “must” do something. In other words, it’s obligatory.
Here are some examples to illustrate the correct use of words:
The amount of the discount may be recognized in full. [The word “may” describes a possibility]
The amount of the discount must be recognized in full. [The word “must” describes an obligation]
A reliable case study framework
The Issue, Analysis, Options, Recommendation framework is a reliable case study framework. You can use this framework to formulate your answers to case study questions.

Gorongosa’s hippo population is a case study of a remarkable recovery across Africa
Hippos also play key ecosystem roles in their wetland environments. Studies elsewhere in Africa have also linked hippo-driven inputs to fish die-offs during drought.
Before Mozambique’s civil war, Gorongosa was among the great wildlife parks of Africa, famous for dense concentrations of large mammals. Hippos that once filled the banks of Gorongosa’s floodplain were no exception.
By 2000, hippos had fallen to roughly 100 individuals, a collapse of roughly 97 percent.
Recovery came through a long-term partnership between the Mozambican government and the Gorongosa Restoration Project, led by the Carr Foundation and now the Gorongosa Project.
As poaching is suppressed and the floodplain intact, the hippo population has grown steadily over the past two decades. The population is now in the thousands, and Gorongosa hippos are playing their key roles in shaping the health of the wetland’s ecology.
Hippos breed slowly compared with many other large herbivores, with females typically producing a single calf at intervals of a couple of years.
Hippos are not currently listed as an endangered species, though they are listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. The total population across sub-Saharan Africa is generally estimated at 115, 1000 to 130, 1000 animals, with a downward trend.
Hippos in Gorongosa’s floodplain still face threats, including pressure at the park boundary and the unpredictable nature of floods and droughts.
The common hippopotamus is vulnerable to poaching, as its size provides lots of meat.
As hippos are a keystone species on the floodplain, changes in their behavior can be expected to have cascading effects on other organisms.
The story of Gorongosa’s hippos is a story of recovery, and one that is far from finished.

Dentists recommend brushing your teeth for a full two minutes, twice a day — yet many people brush for only 30 to 45 seconds. Don’t make this mistake.
Do you brush for a full two minutes? Here’s how to brush your teeth correctly, and what mistakes to avoid:
Why do you need to brush?
Brushing your teeth removes plaque and helps prevent it from building up on teeth. Brushing twice a day is a good step toward keeping your teeth strong and healthy — and your smile bright.
How to brush your teeth
When brushing your teeth, hold your toothbrush at a 45-degree angle to your teeth and gumline, and use small, gentle, circular motions. Brushing too hard or with a hard-bristled toothbrush can damage your teeth and cause painful sensitivity. Brushing in a side-to-side motion can also damage your teeth, so stick with gentle, circular motions.
The best toothbrush for you
Drilling, the ADA recommends electric and manual toothbrushes that have been reviewed for safety and effectiveness, and that bear the ADA Seal of Acceptance on their packaging.
How to brush your teeth correctly
To ensure you brush all your teeth, it’s helpful to divide your mouth into quadrants — upper right, upper left, lower right, lower left — and spend about 30 seconds brushing each area.
Brushing at this angle sweeps plaque away from the teeth without damaging the gums.
Young children should use a smear the size of a grain of rice, while older children and adults should use a pea-sized amount.
How often should you replace your toothbrush?
Toothbrushes should be replaced every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles look frayed. After a few months, the bristles break down and are less effective at removing plaque, so you may not be getting the best clean possible.
Toothbrushes should be replaced after colds and the flu, as they can harbor bacteria and reintroduce them into your mouth.
If you are worried about your toothbrush wearing out, talk to your dentist.
Does it matter how you brush your teeth?
Yes, it does. Brushing your teeth the wrong way can lead to problems, including tooth decay and damage.
Brushing your teeth properly can help you keep your teeth healthy and clean, so pay attention to how you brush.

In 2026, with the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals approaching, progress on SDG 5 is uneven and in many places stalled.
The Global Wo.Men Hub
The hub is a unique meeting place to share knowledge and good practices, but also to support policy-making at global, regional, country or local level.
The hub is an inclusive platform, that values diversity and encourages new perspectives and approaches. The proposed solutions to gender inequality are to be evaluated and adapted based on country needs, and the solutions are to be adapted to local contexts.
The hub aims to:
• have a sustainable impact on the SDG 5 targets
• offer a platform for those who want to learn more about gender equality and how to challenge it
Building a global platform to end gender inequality means having a diverse community of members.
The hub’s solutions for policy-makers to implement the Sustainable Development Goal 5 targets
SDG 5 is to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls. It includes targets on ending discrimination and violence, recognizing unpaid care work, ensuring full participation in leadership, and guaranteeing health and reproductive rights.

We’ve watched the case counts tick across the bottom of the news broadcasts and scrolled past images of overwhelmed hospitals in our social media feeds. Nearly every conversation has returned to the virus. And we must choose how to respond.
With good reason, many of us have panicked. Hand sanitizer sold at many times its usual price.
The panic was contagious, indeed.
The psychology of panic decisions during a pandemic
What’s more, research has shown that panic selling isn’t the result of a logical decision. The brain doesn’t respond well to uncertainty. It’s a shortcoming of our brains that has its roots in evolution.
Between mid-February and late March 2020, the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value. But the exact timing of a market recovery is uncertain.
In 2000, psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West proposed the System 1 / System 2 distinction, which Daniel Kahneman later made famous. System 1 is the brain’s fast-thinking system, while System 2 is the logical, slower-thinking process. In times of panic, our brains switch to System 1 and make snap decisions without much thought.
To err is human
There’s a reason for our tendency to panic. In our evolution, we relied on the snap decision-making ability of System 1 to survive.
But the markets today aren’t much like a sabertooth tiger. We don’t face an immediate threat. The coronavirus won’t eat us.
It’s true that stocks can lose value. But that’s a gradual process, not an immediate threat.
And this makes our tendency to panic all the more frustrating.
But there is a solution.
If we can’t turn off our panic instincts, we can at least account for them.
The answer is to prepare for a market panic in advance. Investors with a written plan made in calm conditions, such as “I will not sell during a drawdown of less than X%,” give their future selves a rule to follow.
They have a system that can override the panic.
Of course, the markets will eventually recover. So why panic?
A pandemic is different
The coronavirus is a global pandemic. So what can we do to prevent ourselves from panicking?
A few tips for navigating the current market:
Be patient. The stock market is a rollercoaster.
Decide in advance. When panic hits, it’s hard to have clarity of mind. And, if we need to, stick to the plan.
The pandemic is scary. It’s easy to want to fill our houses with toilet paper and canned goods to get away from it. But the real panic is not in the world around us but in ourselves.
And, once we acknowledge that we can face our fear — and even overcome it — we’ll be much better equipped to make good decisions.

The Great Famine lasted from 1845 to 1852.
A new strain of the fungus, Tropical Race 4, now threatens Cavendish bananas worldwide.
The blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mold often called late blight. The famine most likely arrived from the Americas in 1845.
Phylloxera is a tiny aphid-like insect that devours the roots of European grapevines. It destroyed a huge share of France's vineyards and devastated winemaking across Europe within a few decades. The wine industry was saved by grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstocks, which drew on a different gene pool.
In 1970, the fungal disease southern corn leaf blight exploited that shared trait and swept the United States. The blight cost about a billion dollars.
Farming across the world has become more specialized and standardized.
The same disease drove Ireland's potato crop into the ground during the great famine.
The reason lies in the nature of modern farming. For much of the twentieth century, the world's export bananas were a single variety, Gros Michel.
The risks of crop monoculture have been well known for decades, but the lure of high yields and easy logistics keep us focused on just a few varieties of each crop.
This disease is caused by a fungus called Fusarium oxysporum.
Genetic variation is nature's way of hedging its bets, and in crops, that variation is diminishing as never before.
The story of this fungus, Phytophthora infestans, which caused the Great Famine, is one of reckless and repeated narrowing of genetic diversity, on a scale that's hard to comprehend.
Corn blight
In the 1960's, the vast majority of US hybrid corn carried the same genetic trait, "Texas male-sterile cytoplasm", which made seed production cheaper.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is one example. Another is the national gene banks run by governments around the world.
There are many examples of the dangers of crop narrowing, and of how to guard against those dangers. Let's start with Ireland. In the autumn of 1845, farmers across Ireland found their potatoes, which had looked healthy just days earlier, rotting into black, foul-smelling slime.
The story of these two fungi, phylloxera and Phytophthora infestans, underscores that growing predominantly one high-yielding variety, as Irish farmers did for much of the last two centuries, could be the best route to ruin. But narrowing a crop's genetic base isn't just a problem for farmers who plant potatoes; it's a problem for all of us.
A fungus called Fusarium oxysporum, which causes Panama disease, tore through plantations in Central America, including in Costa Rica, forcing growers to abandon fields.
When a crop's genetic variation narrows, any disease or pest that targets a shared trait can exploit that weakness sooner or later, as the examples of the Great Famine in Ireland and of phylloxera in France show.
We're repeating these mistakes today.
The potatoes that went into the ground during the Irish potato famine were genetically near-identical. The famine killed roughly one million people.
The same thing has happened with bananas.
Ireland's population fell by around a quarter.

J.P. Morgan, then seventy years old, had summoned the city’s leading bankers and trust company presidents to his private library on Madison Avenue. By some accounts, Morgan locked the doors until the bankers agreed to pool funds and stop the run. In 1912 the House Banking and Currency Committee, chaired by Arsène Pujo, opened hearings into what newspapers called the “Money Trust.” Representative Charles Lindbergh Sr., of Minnesota, father of the aviator, warned that the act established “the most gigantic trust on earth.” Senator Nelson Aldrich of Rhode Island, chairman of the commission, was a Republican power broker whose daughter married John D. Rockefeller Jr. In 1912, Democrats swept the elections, and Senator Aldrich found himself out of power. Wilson’s version of the plan—steered by Representative Carter Glass —was signed by Wilson on December 23, 1913.
Why was a private bank created to control the nation’s money supply? According to the official version, the Panic of 1907 was the catalyst. Depositors stormed the banks across New York, demanding their money. The Aldrich-Vreeland Act of 1908 created a National Monetary Commission, chaired by Senator Aldrich. Over roughly ten days, the commission members drafted the blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve System. At the First National City Bank of New York, Frank Vanderlip, president, was on the guest list. Paul Warburg, partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co., was on the guest list. Henry P. Davison, senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co., was on the guest list. Charles D. Norton, president of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York, was on the guest list. Senator Aldrich also invited Assistant Secretary of the Treasury A.
The others met in secret at the Jekyll Island Club off the coast of Georgia, a winter retreat for families such as the Morgans, Rockefellers, and Vanderbilts. They were instructed to use only first names and to arrive one at a time. The members of the island party included
• Senator Aldrich, Republican of Rhode Island
• Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, A. Piatt Andrew
Vanderlip said that if the meeting had been exposed, the plan “would have had no chance whatever of passing Congress.” The final report of the commission documented that partners and officers of J.P. Morgan & Co., First National Bank, and National City Bank held 341 directorships in 112 corporations. Those corporations controlled more than $22 billion in resources.
Paul Warburg, who had been at Jekyll Island, was appointed to the first Federal Reserve Board.
Member banks still hold stock in the regional Reserve Banks.
The United States had no central bank, and no lender of last resort.

Jesus’ name isn’t a casual expletive for everyone.
But using Jesus’ name as a casual expletive is not uncommon. That’s my point.
Why? Why do some people feel so comfortable using Jesus’ name that way? Perhaps it’s because Jesus’ name is culturally so familiar.
Devout Muslims, for instance, customarily add the blessing “peace be upon him” when they speak or write Muhammad’s name.
By historical record, Jesus lived in first-century Palestine, taught crowds, healed the sick, and was executed under Pontius Pilate. By faith, Jesus claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life, and according to his followers rose from the dead.
But by familiarity, Jesus’ name has become so commonplace that it’s used as a casual expletive.
So let’s try something else. Let’s attempt to increase the familiarity and comfort of the name Jesus, but in a more reverent and respectful way.
Before we do, a little background on Saul of Tarsus.
Saul was brilliant, devout, and zealous, trained in the Jewish law. He believed the growing movement of Jesus’ followers was a dangerous heresy and set out to destroy it. Saul went house to house dragging believers off to prison. He watched as a Christian named Stephen was stoned.
But something happened to Saul on a road to Damascus, according to the book of Acts.
A light from heaven flashed around him, and he fell to the ground. Saul heard a voice say “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
Saul asked “Who are you, Lord?”
Saul was blinded for three days.
Saul believed in Jesus, was baptized, and began to proclaim that Jesus is the Son of God.
Paul wrote that at the name of Jesus “every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).
Reading one of the Gospels is a good place to start, perhaps Mark, the shortest and most direct.
You’ll discover that Jesus is familiar, yes, but also mysterious, and deep, and life-changing, and worthy of reverence and respect.

Gainesville, a college town in north-central Florida, briefly had an experimental renewable-energy policy that attracted global attention.
And now that it has wound down the program, started in early 2009, others are wondering what it can teach about the role of solar energy in the broader US electricity market.
Under the FIT, as it is called, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), the city-owned power company, offered anyone who installed solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years.
And the income was guaranteed for 20 years, even if the cost of electricity from other sources, and the wholesale price GRU could get for power from the rooftop arrays, fell sharply.
By 2014, when the program closed to new projects, Gainesville had added roughly 18 megawatts of solar.
But the program also has become part of a widely cited cautionary tale. Spain, which had greatly expanded its solar capacity under its FIT, then faced rising surcharges and cut its tariffs sharply. Germany, which had made the FIT model famous under its 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act, also faced rising costs, and cut its tariffs sharply.
Gainesville officials, led by Regan, studied the German model and adapted it for a municipal utility.
It is stuck with its existing contracts, which will remain in place for two decades.
GRU capped new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and in some cases, it reduced the tariff for later participants, but the contracts early participants signed stayed locked in for two decades.
In the United States, the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act generally ties what utilities must pay small generators to their "avoided cost," meaning what the power would otherwise have cost them. Under federal law, wholesale power rates fall largely under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
